## Teaching Philosophy

I teach students to think scientifically, evaluate evidence critically, and become increasingly independent learners. My courses combine structured practice, active learning, and scaffolded projects so that students can build difficult skills before using them independently.

Whether or not students continue in psychology, I want them to leave my courses better able to ask good questions, evaluate claims, communicate evidence, and solve problems.

## Courses Taught

### PSY 250: Research Design & Analysis I

**Instructor of Record, Summer 2026**  

I independently developed and taught this introductory research-methods course, including recorded lectures, activities, assignments, exams, grading materials, and a scaffolded research-proposal project. Students move from evaluating published research and searching the literature to developing hypotheses, designing a study, writing an APA-style proposal, and presenting their work. I also supervised two undergraduate teaching assistants.

### PSY 317: Social Psychology Lab

**Instructor of Record, Summer 2024, Fall 2024, Summer 2025, and Summer 2026**  
Fall 2024 included two fully in-person sections; summer offerings were online asynchronous.

This upper-level seminar-style course introduces students to replication, preregistration, open science, questionable research practices, research design, and scientific communication. Students critically evaluate published research and develop a preregistered social-psychology study through discussion, applied activities, group research design, presentations, and scientific writing.

## Additional Teaching Experience

I have served as a graduate teaching assistant for Research Design and Analysis I, Social Psychology, and Research Design and Analysis II/Statistics. Selected guest lectures include Health Psychology at a Glance; Attitudes, Behaviors, and Persuasion; Moderation and Mediation in Psychology; and Springboard Article Discussion and Study Design.

## How I Teach

### Build Independence Through Scaffolding

The PSY 250 research proposal is my clearest example. Students begin by evaluating a springboard article and searching the literature, then develop a research question, hypotheses, and variables. Through outlines, peer review, and instructor feedback, they build individual components before integrating them into a complete research proposal and presentation.

### Teach Students to Trace Claims Back to Evidence

In one activity, students locate popular articles that make claims about detox diets, identify the scientific sources those articles cite, find the original research, and compare what the evidence supports with how the claim is presented publicly. The exercise turns scientific literacy into a concrete habit: follow a claim back to its evidence before deciding what to believe.

### Learn Actively

I use think-pair-share, small-group discussion, student-generated examples, and applied research-design activities to give students repeated opportunities to practice reasoning rather than only listen to explanations. These activities ask students to explain concepts, evaluate evidence, make methodological decisions, and learn from how their classmates approach the same problem.

### Connect Learning to Transferable Skills

Students practice critical thinking, project management, communication, teamwork, public speaking, and evidence evaluation throughout my courses. These skills remain useful whether students continue in psychology, pursue another field, or apply what they have learned outside the classroom.


## Evidence of Teaching Effectiveness

Student feedback across my courses frequently highlights organization, accessibility, engagement, detailed feedback, and opportunities to practice difficult material before completing larger assignments.

> “I liked how the course built up to the final replicability project instead of having us do it all at once. The smaller assignments and discussions helped me understand each part of the research process before putting everything together.”

> “Skylar made the class very engaging, which I deeply enjoyed. Her slides were interactive and I really enjoyed the activities throughout. The content
was also presented in a way that made sense. She always knew how to explain the concepts and topic in a way that was clear and effective.”
